meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 14: MCP Registry
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: What does the official MCP Registry actually store, and who is meant to consume it?

options.text: Server metadata in server.json, consumed mainly by downstream aggregators
Only remote server URLs, consumed by MCP clients at connection time
Signed attestations of server behaviour, consumed by security scanners
Server binaries and container images, consumed directly by host applications

questions.explanation: The registry hosts metadata that points at packages on npm, PyPI, NuGet, crates.io, OCI registries or release assets. It is intended to be consumed by downstream aggregators and marketplaces, which host applications then consume.

questions.question: A team wants to publish under com.acme/*. What must they prove, and how?

options.text: That the package is public on npm, by linking the package URL in server.json
Nothing: reverse-DNS names are advisory and the registry does not verify them
Ownership of the acme GitHub organization, proved through GitHub's OAuth device flow at publish time
Control of acme.com, through a DNS TXT record or a /.well-known/mcp-registry-auth file

questions.explanation: Domain-based namespaces use DNS or HTTP authentication, proving control of the domain with a signed key. GitHub OAuth covers io.github.<user or org>/* namespaces. Namespace authentication is what makes registry names meaningful.

questions.question: You distribute your server as a container image and want to claim its registry name. Where does the claim go?

options.text: In an annotation on the registry entry, signed with your publishing key
In the image entrypoint, which the registry executes once to read the name
In an image label named io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name
In a README layer added to the image, in a mcp-name: line

questions.explanation: Each ecosystem has its own marker: an OCI image carries the io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name label, npm uses the mcpName field in package.json, and PyPI and NuGet use a mcp-name: line in the README. The registry never runs your artifact.

questions.question: A solo developer with no company domain wants to publish. Which namespace is open to them, and what proves the claim?

options.text: io.github.<username>, proved by authenticating as that GitHub account
any namespace they like, since names are first-come, first-served
com.<username>, proved by a DNS TXT record on any domain they control
dev.mcp.<username>, assigned by the registry when the account is created

questions.explanation: Reverse-DNS namespaces need proof of the domain, but io.github.<username> is available to anyone who can authenticate as that GitHub identity. Names are not first-come, first-served: every namespace requires a proof of control.

questions.question: A server is published to PyPI. Which proof of ownership does the registry check?

options.text: An io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name label on the built artifact
An mcp-name: <server name> string in the package README
A DNS TXT record on the publisher's domain
An mcpName field in the package metadata, matching server.json

questions.explanation: PyPI and NuGet use an mcp-name marker in the README, which may be an HTML comment. npm uses the mcpName field in package.json, Docker/OCI uses the io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name annotation, and DNS TXT records authenticate a namespace, not a package.

questions.question: Why can a crates.io publisher not hide the mcp-name marker in an HTML comment, unlike on PyPI?

options.text: crates.io requires the marker in the crate description field, which is rendered without any HTML
crates.io strips HTML comments when rendering the README, so the token must be visible text
crates.io does not render READMEs at all, so the marker must go in Cargo.toml
Cargo packages are verified by signature instead, making the marker unnecessary

questions.explanation: PyPI and NuGet preserve HTML comments in their rendered README, but crates.io strips them during markdown-to-HTML conversion, so the validator never sees the token. Cargo authors must include mcp-name as visible markdown text.

questions.question: An MCPB package entry carries fileSha256. Who verifies that hash?

options.text: The registry, at publish time, rejecting any entry whose recomputed hash does not match
GitHub or GitLab, as part of the release-asset upload
Nobody: it is informational metadata for humans reading server.json
MCP clients, before installing the artifact; the registry itself does not validate it

questions.explanation: The registry does not validate the hash. MCP clients validate it before installation to ensure file integrity, and downstream registries may add their own checks. The MCPB URL must also contain the string 'mcp'.
